title: Mani stones
hookLine: stones carved with mantras, piled along paths and passes

lines: A WALL BESIDE A HIGH TRAIL.
ONE MORE STONE ON THE PILE.
cards: A trail climbs toward a high pass. No trees, thin air, wind that doesn't stop.
Beside the path runs a low wall that isn't really a wall: flat stones stacked together, more than anyone could count at a glance, some gray and plain, some painted blue, red, yellow and white.
Look closer and every one is carved, the same six syllables over and over, cut into rock by hands you'll never meet.
A walker steps to the left so the wall stays on her right, sets one more stone on the pile, and keeps climbing. Today: mani stones.

teach.b: First, what's carved. Mani stones usually carry om mani padme hum, the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion Tibetans call Chenrezig, whom you met back in year one.
Some carry other mantras, a prayer, or an image of a buddha. The name comes from the mantra's second word, mani, a jewel. Second, who makes them.
Skilled stone carvers, who sell or are paid for them. A family marking a death, a birth, a recovery or a hope. A pilgrim with a nail and a lot of patience.

Then they're left where people pass: a pass, a bridge, a crossroads, the edge of a village, around a stupa. Over years the piles grow into long walls, built by strangers who never met. Third, the idea underneath.
Tibetan teachers say a mantra carved in stone keeps sounding.

A prayer flag lets the wind carry its words; a prayer wheel lets the turning hand recite; a mani stone lets the rock do it, quietly, in every weather, for as long as it lasts. That's your line: the stone chants.
Not that a rock has a voice, but that the wish carved into it doesn't stop when the carver goes home. Fourth, how to pass one.

teach.h: KEEP IT ON YOUR RIGHT. ADD, DON'T TAKE.
teach.b: Travelers keep mani walls on their right, the same clockwise respect as yesterday's kora. Stones are added, not taken: taking one home as a souvenir would be taking someone's prayer.
Each new stone joins a long line of strangers' wishes for the beings who will walk this way.

how: In Tibetan Buddhist regions, stones carved with om mani padme hum and other mantras are left at passes, bridges, villages and stupas, where they build up into long mani walls; travelers pass them clockwise, keeping them on the right.

o: stones taken home from a pilgrimage as blessings

games.q: on a high trail you reach a long wall of carved stones. the path splits around it. which way do you go?
o: keep the wall on your right.
keep the wall on your left.
climb over the middle to save time.
games.why: travelers keep mani walls on their right, the same clockwise respect as kora.

practice: Take a stone, a pebble, or even a scrap of paper and a pen, and slowly write one short line on it: om mani padme hum, a line from your own tradition, or one word that holds a wish for others, like kindness.
Write it one letter at a time, as if carving, then hold it for a few breaths. If it's a stone, you might leave it somewhere people pass.

wordCard.voice: Mani stones. Stones carved with mantras, usually om mani padme hum, piled along paths, passes and stupas, and passed with respect on the right. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit mani, a jewel; the second word of om mani padme hum, which gives the stones their name.

carryVoice: Your line: the stone chants. One more stone on the pile, one more wish. Until tomorrow.
